missions.title: Inspect the first item

lesson.heading: Peek at the first piece of gear
lesson.text: The equipment list is in pick-up order. Show what the cartographer should grab first without taking it off the list. If the list is empty, there is nothing to inspect.

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: A list stores an ordered collection. Square brackets create one; `len` counts its elements. Index 0 selects the first element. A missing index raises `IndexError`, so an empty-list contract needs attention before indexing.

missions.brief: Return the first gear label in `items`, or `None` when the list is empty.
requirements: `items` is a list of text values. Return an element, not a one-element list. Leave the supplied list unchanged.
Return the result without printing or reading input inside the helper.
hints: What index describes the first element?
Check whether that index exists before reading it.
Handle the empty case, then retrieve the first value.

missions.title: Inspect the last item

lesson.heading: Read the last travel time
lesson.text: The grimoire records a time after every leg. Retrieve the most recent entry without erasing any of the log. An expedition that has not moved yet has no last reading.

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: Negative indexes count backward from the end: `-1` is the last element, `-2` the one before it. They still require an element to exist. Empty lists have no valid positive or negative indexes.

missions.brief: Return the most recent travel time in `items`, or `None` when the list is empty.
requirements: `items` is a list of integers. Do not remove or change any elements.
Return the result without printing or reading input inside the helper.
hints: You can count from the end without calculating a positive index.
A negative index does not solve the empty-list case.
Return the last value only after ruling out the empty input.

missions.title: Preview part of a queue

lesson.heading: Preview the next stops
lesson.text: The scout wants to see the first few jobs on the expedition route without editing the plan. A short route shows only the jobs it has. Asking for zero should show an empty preview.

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: A slice selects a range of elements: `items[start:stop]` includes `start` and excludes `stop`. Omitting `start` uses the beginning. Slicing beyond the end is safe and returns the elements that exist. A slice creates a new outer list.

missions.brief: Return a new preview containing up to `count` jobs from the start of the expedition queue `jobs`.
requirements: `jobs` is a list of strings and `count` is a non-negative integer. Return all available jobs if count exceeds the length; zero returns an empty list. Do not change `jobs`.
Return the result without printing or reading input inside the helper.
hints: This is an ordered prefix, not a search.
The slice stop is excluded, just like range.
A prefix slice naturally handles a count larger than the available collection.

missions.title: Add to the real queue

lesson.heading: Add a stop to the real route
lesson.text: The crew has agreed to take another survey job. Add it to the shared queue itself so everyone sees the change. The same job label can appear twice when the crew plans two visits.

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: `append` adds one element to the end of a list in place. The method returns `None`; it does not return the changed list. The caller sees the mutation because its name refers to the same list object.
lesson.code:
tasks = ["Gate"]
result = tasks.append("Vault")
print(tasks)   # ['Gate', 'Vault']
print(result)  # None

missions.brief: Add job to the end of the supplied queue, changing that same list.
requirements: `queue` is a list of strings; `job` is a string. Keep all existing jobs in their order and append one job, even if it is a duplicate.
Return `None`. The helper prints nothing. The sample outer code prints the return and then the changed list; checks verify both the return and mutation.
missions.starter:
def enqueue(queue, job):
    pass

sample = ['A']
result = enqueue(sample, 'B')
print(result)
print(sample)
missions.example:
enqueue(['A'], 'B') -> None; arguments afterward: [['A', 'B'], 'B']
enqueue([], 'A') -> None; arguments afterward: [['A'], 'A']
hints: The contract asks for a visible change to the caller's collection.
Reassigning a local name to a new list is different from mutating the supplied list.
append changes the object and already has the required no-value return behavior.

reference.code:
def enqueue(queue, job):
    queue.append(job)

sample = ['A']
result = enqueue(sample, 'B')
print(result)
print(sample)
notes: No explicit `return` is necessary when `None` is the intended result.
Assigning `queue = queue.append(job)` would replace the local name with `None`.

missions.title: Remove the most recent job

lesson.heading: Undo the last route edit
lesson.text: The cartographer added the wrong stop and wants to undo just that addition. Remove the last queued job and return it so the console can say what was removed. An empty route has nothing to undo.

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: `pop` removes and returns an element. With no index, it uses the last element. Popping an empty list raises `IndexError`, so decide the empty behavior before calling it.

missions.title: Number the labels

lesson.heading: Number the gear manifest
lesson.text: A quartermaster calls out equipment by its number on the printed list. Start the numbers at one and keep the original order so the crew can match a printed label to its place.

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: `enumerate` supplies a position and a value together. A `for` loop can bind both names, separated by a comma. The default position starts at zero; `start=1` is useful for human labels. F-strings convert inserted values to text for display.
lesson.code:
for position, word in enumerate(["Lantern", "Rope"], start=1):
    print(f"{position}: {word}")

hints: You need each value and its human-facing number.
`enumerate` can supply both, including the starting number.

missions.title: Check for a complete label

lesson.text: An equipment request has to match a whole label on the crate list. A partial label could send the crew away with the wrong tool. This particular registry preserves case, unlike the movement command parser.

lesson.text: For a list, `in` checks whether an equal element exists. It does not treat each element as a string to search inside. This differs from substring membership in one string.

missions.title: Preview without changing the queue

lesson.heading: Preview a detour safely
lesson.text: The cartographer wants to see how the queue would look with a detour at the end. The party should still see the original route until it agrees to take the detour.

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: `other = items` creates another name for the same list. `items.copy()` creates a separate outer list. With a flat list of strings, this lets a preview add an item without changing the real queue.
lesson.code:
original = ["Gate"]
copy = original.copy()
copy.append("Vault")
print(original)  # ['Gate']
print(copy)      # ['Gate', 'Vault']

missions.brief: Return a preview list containing the existing queue followed by `job`, without changing queue.
requirements: `queue` is a list of strings; `job` is a string. Preserve all existing elements and duplicates. Return a new outer list even when the `queue` is empty.
Return the result without printing or reading input inside the helper.
hints: A second name alone is not a second list.
Your preview must own a separate outer collection.
A copy followed by append, slicing followed by append, or list concatenation can meet the goal.

reference.code:
def preview_add(queue, job):
    preview = queue.copy()
    preview.append(job)
    return preview

print(preview_add(['A'], 'B'))
notes: Copying separates later outer-list mutation.
This is a shallow copy: nested mutable objects would still be shared. The current contract contains only strings.

missions.title: Build a clean queue report
missions.concepts: Chapter project - filtering, totals and list contracts

lesson.heading: Approve the survey queue
lesson.text: The crew has a list of planned survey times and a limited watch. Count the valid jobs, add only their durations, and report whether the whole queue fits. Two jobs taking the same time still use two slots.

lesson.heading: The idea
lesson.text: Combine a collection rule with a small report. Decide which values represent real jobs before counting and totaling them. Keep the original collection available for the caller.

missions.brief: Report the usable survey jobs in the expedition queue and whether they fit the available time.
requirements: `lengths` is a list of integers; `available` is a non-negative integer. Only positive lengths represent usable jobs. Keep duplicates as separate jobs.

Return exactly `Queued: N | Total: T min | Fits: B` using the count and sum of usable jobs. Fits includes equality. Empty or all-invalid input means zero jobs and zero total, which fits any supplied budget.
Do not change `lengths`. You may use helpers or any equivalent valid implementation.
Return the result without printing or reading input inside the helper.
missions.example:
queue_report([10, 0, -2, 20], 30) -> 'Queued: 2 | Total: 30 min | Fits: True'
queue_report([], 0) -> 'Queued: 0 | Total: 0 min | Fits: True'
hints: The filter determines both which jobs count and which durations contribute.
An empty accepted collection should still have a sensible count and total.
Separate filtering, aggregation and display if combining them makes debugging harder.

tests.hint: Compare the result with the visible contract, especially the boundary or empty-input rule.

tests.label: queue_report example 2

reference.code:
def queue_report(lengths, available):
    valid = [length for length in lengths if length > 0]
    total = 0
    for length in valid:
        total = total + length
    return f"Queued: {len(valid)} | Total: {total} min | Fits: {total <= available}"

print(queue_report([10, 0, -2, 20], 30))
notes: Filtering once gives count and total the same definition of a valid job.
A single loop that counts and sums accepted values avoids an intermediate list and is equally valid.
